passage:
Friday
Today I finally did it. On Tuesday I lost Tenzin's earphones at the swimming pool, and for three days I dodged him. Kept saying I'd "check at home". Felt awful every time he looked at me.
This morning before assembly I just said it: "I lost them at the pool. I'm sorry. I'll pay you back from my pocket money in two weeks."
He stared for a second, then laughed. "Bro, I thought you were angry with me for three days!"
Then he said, "And my charger that stopped working, that was you too, right?" I said no, I never touched the charger, but the earphones were totally on me. He thought about it and said okay.
We ate lunch together like normal. Honestly, three days of hiding felt worse than one minute of sorry.
Karthik

qa.q: Where did Karthik lose Tenzin's earphones?
qa.a: Karthik lost them at the swimming pool.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel during the three days of dodging?
qa.a: Karthik felt awful every time Tenzin looked over, weighed down by guilt and the effort of hiding.

qa.q: Which part of Karthik's apology worked, and why?
qa.a: Karthik said plainly what happened, apologised and offered to pay back in two weeks, then calmly refused blame for the charger, owning the real mistake without taking all the fault.

qa.q: What had the three days been like for Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin thought Karthik was angry with him, so the dodging was more confusing and hurtful than the lost earphones.

grounding: A student owns losing Tenzin's earphones with a plain sorry, declines blame for the charger, and finds things back to normal by lunch.

Bhupen: my cousin came over, what was i supposed to do
Santosh: text me?? i waited at the ground till 5
Bhupen: u always make a big deal
Bhupen: [message deleted]
Bhupen: ok wait. that's not fair of me
Bhupen: i forgot to text. that's on me. sorry
Bhupen: can i buy u a samosa tomorrow? and i'll be at next sunday's match by 3

Bhupen: i know. i messed up. i'll tell the team it was my fault, not ur planning

Bhupen: done
Bhupen looked at the screen for a while. It had taken ten seconds to type sorry, and the knot in his stomach was already loosening.

qa.q: Until what time did Santosh wait at the ground?
qa.a: Santosh waited at the ground till 5.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's deleted message suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he caught himself mid-defence, feeling a flash of guilt as he saw that blaming Santosh was not fair.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the chat, and why did it help?
qa.a: Typing "ok wait, that's not fair of me" and then owning the mistake ended the defensiveness; with a concrete way to make up, Santosh softened within a few lines.

qa.q: What would change if Bhupen had kept saying Santosh makes a big deal?
qa.a: Santosh would feel dismissed twice, first by the no-show and then by the blame, and the friendship might cool instead of ending with extra chutney.

grounding: A boy starts to defend missing a birthday match, catches himself, owns the mistake with a plain sorry, and finds the friendship recovers quickly.

passage:
In the village, Alka's bicycle was her pride. She'd saved for the silver bell herself. So when Anirban borrowed the bike to fetch medicine for his grandmother and came back with the bell hanging loose and scratched, he knew what was coming.
Alka stared at it. "What happened?"
Anirban felt the usual excuses rise: the road was bad, a dog chased him, the bell was loose already. Some of that was true. The road was bad.
But he'd also been riding too fast, showing off to the boys at the well.
"I was going too fast and hit a stone," he said. "I'm sorry. I'll fix the bell tomorrow at the cycle shop."
Alka's face relaxed a little. "The road near the well is terrible, though."
"It is. But I was still too fast."
She laughed, surprised. The next evening, they rode together to the cycle shop.

qa.q: Why did Anirban borrow the bicycle?
qa.a: To fetch medicine for his grandmother.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel as the excuses rose in him?
qa.a: Anirban felt nervous and tempted to defend himself, but chose honesty about riding too fast.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Anirban owned his part with a plain sorry and offered to fix the bell, which helped the friendship recover quickly.

qa.q: How did Alka react to Anirban's apology?
qa.a: Alka relaxed, even acknowledged the bad road, and laughed in surprise at his honesty.

grounding: It shows a teenager owning his part in damaging a friend's bike with a plain sorry, finding the friendship recovers faster than through defensiveness.

passage:
At the secondary school in Rome, the whole class knew about Yosef's failed audition by lunchtime. Lucia had said, laughing at the lockers, "He sounded like a goat." It had spread from there, with others adding worse.
Yosef found her after school. "Why would you say that?"
Lucia's first instinct was to shrug: everyone was joking, others said worse, he was too sensitive. She felt the words ready on her tongue.
Instead she said, "I said the goat thing. That was mean, and I'm sorry. I didn't say the other stuff, and I'll tell people to stop."
Yosef blinked. He'd expected an argument. "Okay," he said slowly. "Thanks."
The next day, when someone started the goat noise in the corridor, Lucia said loudly, "Leave it. I started that, and I shouldn't have."
By Friday, Yosef was sitting with her group at lunch again.

qa.q: What did Lucia say Yosef sounded like?
qa.a: He sounded like a goat.

qa.q: How did Lucia feel when Yosef confronted her?
qa.a: Lucia felt defensive at first, with excuses ready, but chose to admit her part instead.

qa.q: How did Lucia take responsibility without accepting all blame?
qa.a: She apologised for the goat comment she made but was clear she didn't say the other things, and then asked people to stop.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel when Lucia apologised?
qa.a: Yosef felt surprised and relieved, having expected an argument, and by Friday he sat with her group again.

grounding: It shows a teenager owning her own hurtful remark with a plain sorry while not accepting blame for what others said, and the friendship recovering.

passage:
In the sports academy's under-17 football match on Saturday, Sachin had the ball in front of goal and Wasim was wide open. Sachin shot anyway. Missed. They lost by one.
In the dressing room, Wasim said quietly, "I was free."
Sachin snapped, "You were offside anyway." He wasn't. Sachin knew it. Everyone knew it.
All weekend, the team felt split. Sachin's roommate in the hostel said nothing at dinner. Wasim sat at another table.
On Monday morning before training, Sachin found Wasim tying his boots.
"Wasim. You were onside. I should have passed. I wanted the goal. I'm sorry."
Wasim looked up. "You also didn't miss the easy one in the first half. That was good." He stood up. "Next time, pass."
"Next time, I'll pass."
The coach, watching from the gate, said nothing, but at training that day, the team was loud again.

qa.q: What did Sachin claim about Wasim in the dressing room?
qa.a: That Wasim was offside anyway.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel over the weekend?
qa.a: Sachin felt uneasy and isolated, knowing his excuse was false and seeing the team split.

qa.q: What did Sachin do on Monday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He admitted he should have passed and said a plain sorry, which quickly repaired things with Wasim and the team.

qa.q: How did Wasim respond to Sachin's apology?
qa.a: Wasim accepted it warmly, even praising something Sachin did well, and asked him simply to pass next time.

grounding: It shows a teenager replacing defensiveness with a plain sorry after a selfish shot, and the team relationship recovering quickly.

passage:
Dear Vinita didi,
Remember in June when Rhea and I didn't talk for a whole month because I kept arguing that the scooty dent wasn't really my fault? You said next time, try just saying sorry and see what happens. I tried it this week.
I posted a group photo from the picnic where Kavin had his eyes half shut and food on his shirt. He messaged me, really upset. My first reply was already typed: "It's just a photo, chill." I deleted it. I wrote: "You're right, I should have asked. Sorry. I've taken it down."
He called me something rude in his first message, and I did tell him that part wasn't okay. But I didn't pretend the photo was his fault.
By evening he sent a funny sticker and we were normal again. One day instead of one month!
Love,
Ira

qa.q: What reply had Ira typed before deleting it?
qa.a: “It's just a photo, chill.”

qa.q: How did Ira feel about how quickly things recovered with Kavin?
qa.a: Ira felt relieved and pleased, even surprised, that a plain sorry fixed things in one day instead of one month.

qa.q: How did Ira balance owning the mistake with not taking all the blame?
qa.a: Ira apologised plainly and took the photo down, but also told Kavin his rude word wasn't okay, taking responsibility without accepting blame that wasn't Ira's.

qa.q: How might Kavin have felt if he had received the first reply?
qa.a: Kavin would likely have felt dismissed and more hurt, and the quarrel might have dragged on like the month with Rhea.

grounding: Shows a teenager owning a mistake with a plain sorry and finding the friendship recovers faster than it did through defensiveness.
